facts.fact: The First Buddhist Council was held in 483 BCE at Rajagriha.
The First Council was patronised by Ajatashatru.
The First Council was presided over by Mahakassapa.
The First Council compiled the Vinaya Pitaka (recited by Upali) and the Sutta Pitaka (recited by Ananda).
At the First Council Upali recited the Vinaya and Ananda the Sutta.
The Second Buddhist Council was held in 383 BCE at Vaishali.
The Second Council was patronised by Kalashoka.
The Second Council was presided over by Sabbakami.
The Second Council addressed corruption in the Sangha and reaffirmed monastic discipline.
The Third Buddhist Council was held in 250 BCE at Pataliputra.
The Third Council was patronised by Ashoka.
The Third Council was presided over by Moggaliputta Tissa.
The Third Council established Theravada, compiled the Abhidhamma Pitaka and sent missionaries abroad.
Moggaliputta Tissa composed the Kathavatthu at the Third Council.
The Fourth Buddhist Council was held in the 1st century CE in Kashmir.
The Fourth Council was patronised by Kanishka.
The Fourth Council was presided over by Vasumitra, with Ashvaghosha as deputy.
The Fourth Council divided Buddhism into Mahayana and Hinayana and adopted Sanskrit for the scriptures.
A Buddhist council is called a Sangiti (communal recitation).
At the Second Council the Sangha split into the Sthaviravadins and the Mahasanghikas.
Hinayana means 'the Lesser Path'; Theravada means 'Doctrine of the Elders'.
Hinayana treats the Buddha as a human and discourages idol worship.
Hinayana scriptures are in Pali.
Hinayana seeks individual salvation (Nirvana) through self-discipline and meditation.
Hinayana is practised today in Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Thailand.
Ashoka was a significant patron of Hinayana.
Mahayana means 'the Greater Path' and arose later than Hinayana.
The source calls Mahayana a heterodox school.
Mahayana treats the Buddha as divine and worships the Buddha and Bodhisattvas as idols.
Mahayana believes in universal liberation of all beings.
Mahayana scriptures are in Sanskrit, and it emphasises mantras.
Mahayana is practised today in China and Japan.
Kanishka was the notable patron of Mahayana.
Vajrayana means 'Vehicle of the Thunderbolt' and is also called Tantric Buddhism.
Vajrayana emphasises the Two Truths Doctrine (conventional and ultimate truth).
Vajrayana uses a symbolic language called Sandhya-bhasa.
Vajrayana worships fierce deities like Tara and stresses the Guru (Lama).
Vajrayana arose in Bengal and Bihar and gained prominence in the 11th century.
Vajrayana is popular in Tibet, Nepal, Bhutan and Mongolia.
The Paramitas are the perfections a Bodhisattva cultivates on the path to Buddhahood.
The Mahasanghika school's deification of the Buddha fostered Mahayana.
The Sthaviravadins belonged to Hinayana, not Mahayana.
Lokottaravada, a Mahasanghika branch, saw the Buddha as supramundane; its Mahavastu is a Sanskrit life of the Buddha.
Sarvastivada, Sautrantika and Sammitiya were Buddhist (not Jain) schools.
Sarvastivada held that past, present and future all exist.
Nagarjuna founded the Madhyamika school, which taught Shunyata (emptiness).
Asanga and Vasubandhu were the thinkers of the Yogachara school.
Buddhist religious literature is collectively the Tripitaka (Three Baskets).
The Vinaya Pitaka gives the rules of discipline for monks and nuns.
The Sutta Pitaka contains the sermons and stories of the Buddha.
The Abhidhamma Pitaka deals with philosophy and metaphysics.
The Dighanikaya is a collection of long discourses in the Sutta Pitaka.
The Jataka tales tell of the Buddha's previous births.
The Therigatha contains the verses of the elder nuns.
The Buddhacharita was written by Ashvaghosha.
'Nirgrantha' (listed in the source among Buddhist texts) is actually the Jain term for Jain ascetics, not a Buddhist text.
Nalanda, Taxila, Valabhi and Vikramasila grew from Buddhist monasteries into centres of learning.
The Milinda Panho is a dialogue between the Indo-Greek king Menander and the monk Nagasena.
The Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa are Pali chronicles of Sri Lanka.
The Divyavadana and Avadanashataka are Sanskrit avadana (legend) collections.
The Nettipakarana is a Buddhist (not Jain) text (UPSC 2022).
The Lalitavistara is a Mahayana life of the Buddha.
Buddhaghosa wrote the Visuddhimagga in Sri Lanka.
Nalanda was founded by the Gupta king Kumaragupta I in the 5th century CE.
Nalanda was destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khilji around 1193 CE.
Vikramashila was founded by the Pala king Dharmapala.
The Chinese pilgrim Hiuen Tsang studied at Nalanda.
Odantapuri was another Pala-era Buddhist vihara.
Bodhisattvas are enlightened beings of Mahayana who stay in samsara to help others attain enlightenment.
The famous Bodhisattva Padmapani painting is at Ajanta (UPSC 2017).
Avalokiteshvara is associated with the Buddha Amitabha.
Samantabhadra forms the Shakyamuni Trinity with Gautama Buddha and Manjushri.
Kshitigarbha also protects children who died young and serves between the Buddha and Maitreya.
Manjushri embodies wisdom and holds a blazing sword.
Avalokiteshvara (Padmapani) embodies infinite compassion and holds a lotus.
Vajrapani represents the power and energy of all Buddhas.
Kshitigarbha vowed to save all beings, including those in hell.
Akashagarbha is revered for cleansing sins.
Samantabhadra is known for his ten vows.
Sarvanivarana-Vishkambhin purifies obstacles on the path.
Maitreya is the future Buddha, yet to come.
The Dharmachakra mudra (Wheel of Dharma) is shown by the Dhyani Buddha Vairochana.
The Dharmachakra mudra signifies Wheel of Dharma.
The Bhumisparsha mudra (earth-witness) is shown by the Dhyani Buddha Akshobhya.
The Bhumisparsha mudra signifies earth-witness.
The Varada mudra (compassion) is shown by the Dhyani Buddha Ratnasambhava.
The Varada mudra signifies compassion.
The Dhyana mudra (meditation) is shown by the Dhyani Buddha Amitabha.
The Dhyana mudra signifies meditation.
The Abhaya mudra (fearlessness) is shown by the Dhyani Buddha Amoghasiddhi.
The Abhaya mudra signifies fearlessness.
Gandhara art shows Greco-Roman influence and realistic Buddha images.
Mathura art is an indigenous Indian style focused on Buddha images and yakshas.
The Amaravati school is known for delicate narrative carvings.
Gandhara sculpture used grey schist, Mathura red sandstone and Amaravati white marble.
Gandhara and Mathura art flourished under the Kushanas; Amaravati under the Satavahanas.
A stupa is a hemispherical shrine built to house relics of the Buddha.
A stupa symbolises the enlightened mind of the Buddha.
Stupas evolved in India from burial mounds in the 6th century BCE.
Ashoka erected 84,000 stupas after the Third Buddhist Council.
The square base of a stupa symbolises Earth.
The hemispherical dome (anda) of a stupa symbolises Water.
The Harmika (small square platform) of a stupa symbolises Fire.
The Yasti (central pole) of a stupa symbolises Air.
The Chattras (umbrella/spire) of a stupa symbolise Space.
Relic stupas enshrine relics of the Buddha or his disciples.
Object stupas contain sacred objects representing the teachings.
Commemorative stupas mark important events in the Buddha's life.
Symbolic stupas represent aspects of Buddhist theology such as enlightenment.
Votive stupas are erected by devotees as devotion or to mark a pilgrimage.
The Sanchi Stupa (Madhya Pradesh) was originally commissioned by Ashoka.
Boudhanath Stupa (Kathmandu, Nepal) is a major centre of Tibetan Buddhism.
Shwedagon (Yangon) is the most sacred pagoda of Myanmar.
The Mahabodhi stupa stands at Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha was enlightened.
Bharhut is another famous early stupa (Madhya Pradesh).
In Sri Lanka stupas are called dagobas.
In Tibet stupas are called chortens.
In East Asia stupas became pagodas (tall tiered towers).
A chaitya is a prayer hall; a vihara is a monastery where monks lived.
Ajanta, Ellora and Bhaja are rock-cut caves with Buddhist murals and sculptures.
The Ajanta caves are cut into a gorge of the Waghora river.
At Ellora, Caves 1–12 are Buddhist.
Karle (Karla) has the largest rock-cut chaitya hall in India.
Tabo monastery is in Spiti (Himachal Pradesh) and Alchi in Ladakh (UPSC 2014).
Kanganahalli (Karnataka) yielded the 'Ranyo Ashoka' inscription with Ashoka's sculpted portrait (UPSC 2019).
The Lion Capital of Ashoka's Sarnath Pillar is India's national emblem.
The Sarnath Lion Capital was adopted as the national emblem on 26 January 1950.
Yakshas (male earth spirits) and Yakshis (female fertility spirits) appear in Buddhist art at sites like Sanchi.
Buddhism spread across North India through the missionary activity of the Sangha.
Ashoka embraced Buddhism after the Kalinga War.
Ashoka sent missionaries to Sri Lanka, Greece, Myanmar, Thailand and Central Asia.
Ashoka's Edicts promoted the Buddha's teachings and outlined the Dhamma (moral code).
Ashoka sent his son Mahinda and daughter Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka.
Ashoka, Kanishka, the Satavahanas, Rashtrakutas and Chalukyas were royal patrons of Buddhism.
Buddhism declined in India but flourished in East Asia (China, Japan) and Southeast Asia (Thailand, Myanmar, Sri Lanka).
Corruption of the Sangha and the rise of ritualism contributed to the decline of Buddhism.
Fragmentation into Hinayana, Mahayana, Vajrayana and Tantrayana sects weakened Buddhism.
The source lists Tantrayana as a fourth sect alongside Hinayana, Mahayana and Vajrayana.
Muslim invasions of the 12th century CE and the Brahmanical revival led to the destruction of monasteries.
Loss of royal patronage, as later kings favoured Brahmanism, hastened the decline.
Ashoka's patronage spread Buddhism and was never a cause of its decline.
The Archaeological Site of Nalanda Mahavihara (Bihar) was inscribed by UNESCO in 2016.
Nalanda was established in the 5th century CE.
The Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi were inscribed by UNESCO in 1989.
The Sanchi Stupa was commissioned by Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE.
The Mahabodhi Temple Complex at Bodh Gaya was inscribed by UNESCO in 2002.
The Ajanta Caves (Aurangabad, Maharashtra) were inscribed by UNESCO in 1983.
The Ajanta caves date back to about the 2nd century BCE.
Buddhism's Ahimsa influenced Indian culture and later Mahatma Gandhi.
Pali and Prakrit flourished through Buddhist teaching and scriptures.
Nalanda, Taxila and Vikramashila drew scholars from abroad.
The Amaravati (Dhanyakataka) Mahachaitya in AP was a Satavahana-era great stupa with marble railings.
Nagarjunakonda (Vijayapuri), capital of the Ikshvakus, was a major Buddhist centre in AP.
The Bhattiprolu stupa yielded a relic casket with an early Brahmi inscription.
Thotlakonda and Bavikonda are Buddhist hill monasteries near Visakhapatnam.
Sankaram (Bojjannakonda) near Anakapalli has rock-cut stupas.
Salihundam (Srikakulam) has Buddhist stupas on the Vamsadhara.
Guntupalli (Eluru district) has rock-cut circular chaitya caves.
Ghantasala (Krishna district) was a Buddhist stupa site and port.
The Kalachakra initiation was held at Amaravati in 2006.
